title: Liver Tests in GI Disease: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Function Are Different Axes
bottomLine: A liver panel contains tests with different jobs. AST/ALT primarily reflect hepatocellular injury, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin help characterize cholestasis/bile handling, and INR/albumin contribute synthetic-function information in context. Pattern and clinical status matter more than lab height alone.
recognize: Predominant AST/ALT elevation suggests a hepatocellular pattern; predominant alkaline-phosphatase elevation with hepatobiliary confirmation suggests cholestatic/infiltrative disease.
Advanced fibrosis can exist with normal ALT, and falling aminotransferases do not guarantee recovery during severe acute liver injury.
differentiate: Albumin is influenced by inflammation, nutrition and renal/GI loss and changes slowly, so it is not a specific acute-liver-failure marker.
ALP can come from liver, bone or placenta; bilirubin can rise in both hepatocellular and cholestatic disease.
assessment: Assess symptoms, hemodynamics, mental status, bleeding, jaundice/pruritus, alcohol, medication/supplement/toxin exposure, metabolic risk, pregnancy and infection/autoimmune clues.
workup: Classify the biochemical pattern first, then order cause-directed viral, toxic, autoimmune, metabolic testing and imaging.
Use ultrasound for cholestatic/obstructive patterns and fibrosis-risk tools such as FIB-4 in appropriate MASLD populations; do not repeat enzymes indefinitely without a diagnostic question.
management: Treat cause and severity simultaneously, stop avoidable hepatotoxic exposure when appropriate, urgently manage obstruction/infection and escalate suspected acute liver failure.
Stable chronic disease requires fibrosis/risk management rather than liver-enzyme chasing.
medicationSafety: Medication decisions depend on the actual hepatic disease and drug; a minor isolated enzyme rise is not automatic proof of drug injury.
Review acetaminophen and supplements carefully during acute injury.
counselling: Explain that 'liver function tests' mix injury, bile-flow and synthetic markers and should not be interpreted as one pass/fail number.
followUp: Trend only the abnormalities that answer a clinical question and ensure persistent/high-risk patterns receive definitive fibrosis/etiology evaluation.
examTrap: Declaring improvement because AST/ALT are falling while INR and mental status are worsening.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job: injury, bile flow and synthetic function are not interchangeable.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Medical/Clinical Biochemistry and Hepatology recommendations

title: GI Tumour Markers: Monitoring Tools, Not Screening Diagnoses
bottomLine: Most GI serum tumour markers are not appropriate stand-alone screening or diagnostic tests in asymptomatic patients. CEA, CA 19-9 and AFP have selected roles in prognosis, treatment monitoring or surveillance when a specific cancer/risk pathway is already established; interpret trends with imaging, pathology and clinical context rather than treating a marker elevation as cancer.
recognize: CEA has established roles in selected colorectal-cancer prognosis/surveillance and treatment-response monitoring after diagnosis.
CA 19-9 can be elevated in pancreatic/biliary malignancy but also cholestasis/inflammation and is not a population screening test.
AFP is used selectively in hepatocellular-carcinoma risk/diagnostic pathways but does not replace imaging or establish HCC alone.
differentiate: Benign inflammation, obstruction, smoking and other conditions can elevate tumour markers.
A normal marker does not exclude malignancy and an elevated marker without a compatible clinical/imaging diagnosis does not establish malignancy.
assessment: Clarify whether the patient has a known cancer, a high-risk surveillance condition or only nonspecific symptoms/anxiety before ordering a marker.
Review liver/biliary disease and smoking when interpreting CEA/CA 19-9 abnormalities.
workup: Use diagnostic imaging/endoscopy/pathology for suspected cancer based on the clinical syndrome; order tumour markers only when the result has a validated management role.
Do not serially repeat unexplained mildly elevated markers as a substitute for establishing a diagnosis.
management: For known cancer, follow the oncology surveillance/treatment protocol and interpret marker trends together with imaging and symptoms.
For incidental marker elevation without a validated indication, stop reflex testing and return to an evidence-based diagnostic pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not expose patients to repeated invasive tests solely because a nonspecific tumour marker is mildly abnormal without corroborating risk/evidence.
redFlags: Cancer alarm symptoms requiring diagnostic workup
Rapid clinical deterioration despite stable marker
Known cancer with rising marker plus compatible symptoms/imaging
counselling: Explain that tumour markers are often monitoring tools and can be abnormal for noncancer reasons.
followUp: Ensure surveillance ownership and interval come from the diagnosed cancer/high-risk pathway, not from the marker number alone.
examTrap: Ordering CEA or CA 19-9 as a general screening test for an asymptomatic patient and interpreting an elevation as cancer.
oneLinePearl: Tumour markers usually follow a diagnosis; they rarely make one by themselves.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada General Surgery recommendations on CEA

title: Endoscopy: Scope When the Result Will Change Care
bottomLine: Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are high-value when used for alarm symptoms, bleeding, abnormal screening follow-up, surveillance, biopsy or therapeutic intervention; they are low-value when used reflexively for uncomplicated low-risk symptoms that have an evidence-based noninvasive first step. Every endoscopy result needs a pathology/action/recall owner.
recognize: Upper-endoscopy indications include GI bleeding, dysphagia/food impaction, selected refractory/alarm dyspepsia/GERD, celiac/structural questions and surveillance pathways.
Colonoscopy indications include positive stool screening, bleeding/anemia/alarm symptoms, IBD/CRC surveillance and polyp/cancer follow-up.
differentiate: Average-risk FIT screening is different from diagnostic colonoscopy and post-polypectomy surveillance.
Choosing Wisely Canada advises against routine endoscopy for low-risk dyspepsia and against colonoscopy solely for constipation in younger patients without alarms/family risk.
assessment: Clarify the question, urgency, bleeding/anemia/weight loss/dysphagia, prior pathology, bowel prep feasibility, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, sedation risk and patient goals.
workup: Use endoscopy when direct visualization/biopsy/therapy is required; use noninvasive H. pylori/celiac/stool/inflammatory/imaging tests first when they answer the question more safely.
Retrieve prior pathology and exam quality before scheduling surveillance.
management: Ensure appropriate bowel prep, peri-procedural medication plan and sedation assessment.
After endoscopy, assign responsibility for pathology, H. pylori treatment, polyp interval, Barrett/IBD surveillance or cancer referral rather than treating the procedure itself as completion.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic interruption is procedure- and thrombotic-risk specific and should follow current periendoscopic guidance.
Sedation risk increases with frailty, OSA, respiratory disease and concurrent sedatives/opioids.
redFlags: Severe colitis/toxic megacolon where routine colonoscopy may be unsafe
counselling: Explain the diagnostic/therapeutic goal, preparation and what follow-up will happen after pathology returns.
followUp: Close pathology and recall loops; new alarm symptoms override a routine surveillance interval.
examTrap: Ordering endoscopy because the patient is anxious despite a low-risk syndrome with a recommended noninvasive first step.
oneLinePearl: A scope is useful when you can say what question it will answer and what you will do with the result.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Guideline Library

title: Nutritional Assessment: Diagnose the Deficit Before Prescribing the Supplement
bottomLine: Nutrition assessment is not a serum-albumin test. Evaluate weight trajectory, intake, GI losses/malabsorption, muscle/function, food access, disease burden and specific deficiency risk, then use food/oral/enteral/parenteral support according to gut function and clinical severity. Refeeding risk must be recognized before aggressively feeding severe malnutrition.
recognize: Unintentional weight loss, reduced intake, muscle wasting, weakness, micronutrient deficiency, chronic diarrhea/steatorrhea and high-output GI losses indicate nutritional risk.
Albumin/prealbumin fall with inflammation and illness and should not be used alone to diagnose protein-calorie malnutrition.
differentiate: Iron, B12, folate, vitamin D and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies have different causes and replacement strategies.
Enteral feeding uses a functional GI tract; parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients who cannot adequately absorb/use the gut despite appropriate enteral strategies.
assessment: Assess recent weight percentage change, intake, swallowing, dentition, nausea/vomiting/diarrhea, surgery, alcohol, medications, food insecurity, muscle/function, pregnancy and disease-specific needs.
workup: Order deficiency-specific CBC/ferritin/B12/folate/electrolytes/magnesium/phosphate/vitamin or other testing when risk and symptoms support it.
In severe malnutrition, check and monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium closely when refeeding begins.
management: Prefer oral food/fortification and oral nutrition supplements when safe and sufficient; use enteral feeding when the gut works but intake is inadequate.
Use parenteral nutrition for intestinal failure or when enteral intake/absorption cannot meet needs, with specialist nutrition support.
Treat the underlying malabsorptive/inflammatory disease rather than relying on supplements alone.
medicationSafety: High-dose supplements can cause toxicity/interactions; iron, calcium and magnesium affect absorption of multiple medications.
Refeeding without electrolyte/thiamine-risk planning can precipitate dangerous shifts.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing food-access and weight language and involve a dietitian when disease complexity or restrictive diets increase risk.
followUp: Track weight/function/intake and targeted deficiencies rather than repeatedly ordering nonspecific nutrition biomarkers.
examTrap: Diagnosing malnutrition solely from a low albumin in a septic patient—or giving aggressive calories to a severely malnourished patient without refeeding precautions.
oneLinePearl: Nutrition care starts with intake, trajectory, function and absorption—not albumin alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Nutrition SIG/resources
Canadian clinical nutrition and refeeding practice principles

title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Replace Losses, Maximize Adaptation, Prevent Intestinal-Failure Complications
bottomLine: Short bowel syndrome is clinically defined by inadequate intestinal absorptive capacity after resection/disease; anatomy matters—remaining small-bowel length, colon continuity and ileum versus jejunum determine fluid, nutrient, bile-salt and medication problems. Management prioritizes hydration/electrolytes, oral/enteral adaptation, targeted antimotility/antisecretory therapy and specialist intestinal-failure support, with parenteral nutrition only as needed.
recognize: High-output diarrhea/stoma, dehydration, magnesium/electrolyte loss, weight loss and vitamin/mineral deficiency are common.
Loss of terminal ileum increases B12/bile-salt issues; lack of colon reduces fluid/salvage capacity; extensive small-bowel loss may produce chronic intestinal failure.
differentiate: High-output ostomy from infection, obstruction or medication can worsen SBS and should not automatically be attributed to baseline anatomy.
Parenteral nutrition dependence is not inevitable; intestinal adaptation and anatomy-specific oral/enteral strategies can reduce support over time.
assessment: Document exact anatomy/surgery, stoma/diarrhea volume, oral intake, urine output, weight, thirst, medications, renal stones, gallstones, line complications and nutrition deficiencies.
workup: Trend renal function, sodium/potassium/magnesium/phosphate, CBC/iron/B12/folate/fat-soluble vitamins and other deficiencies according to anatomy and support.
Monitor liver tests and central-line complications in parenteral-nutrition-dependent patients.
management: Use oral rehydration solution and diet tailored to anatomy rather than excessive plain hypotonic fluid in high-output states.
Use antimotility and acid-suppression/other pharmacotherapy when indicated to reduce losses and improve absorption; avoid unnecessary medication formulations that are poorly absorbed.
Refer complex intestinal failure for multidisciplinary nutrition/GI/surgical care, including parenteral support and selected intestinotrophic therapy/transplant evaluation.
medicationSafety: Drug absorption can be unpredictable with rapid transit/resection; extended-release/enteric-coated formulations may be unreliable.
Central venous parenteral nutrition carries bloodstream-infection, thrombosis and liver/metabolic risks requiring structured monitoring.
counselling: Teach anatomy-specific fluid/ORS strategy, urine-output goals, medication-formulation issues and early line/infection warning symptoms.
followUp: Track hydration, nutrition, deficiencies, renal/liver complications and progress toward enteral autonomy with intestinal-failure specialists.
examTrap: Telling a patient with a very high-output short-bowel stoma simply to drink more plain water, which can worsen sodium/fluid losses.
oneLinePearl: In short bowel, anatomy predicts the loss—and the fluid/nutrition strategy must match the anatomy.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology nutrition/intestinal-failure resources
